utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Case Number IT-95-14-PT, the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Good morning, may I have appearances for counsel, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I am Mark Harmon and appearing with me is Mr Gregory Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And for Bosnia-Herzegovina? MRS VIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and I am the Embassy Counsel for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am appearing here on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina. MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honour. My name is Slokovic Glumac. I am an attorney of law from Zagreb and I am a representative of Mr Ante Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: On February 28th, I entered an order after a hearing on that day. Present was Mrs Glumac as well as Madam Vidovic and for the Prosecution Mr Harmon and I entered an order on that day directing that Mr Jelavic inform me by March 4th of the exact location or locations of the documents that were contained in the subpoena duces tecum, and that he notify me no later than March 4th of the location of those documents. Further, I directed that Mr Jelavic produce the documents that were described in the subpoena duces tecum no later than Wednesday, March 5th, and alternatively directed that Mr Jelavic provide the Prosecutor with immediate access to the documents contained in the Central Archive of what was formerly the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna by March 6th 1997 at 5.00 pm, and I further ordered that, if Mr Jelavic failed to do those things, that is notify me by March 4th of the location and, further, even provide the documents by March 5th or direct the Prosecutor to the location of these documents, that we would have a hearing for Mr Jelavic to show cause why he should not be held in contempt. So we are here for that purpose. I did receive a letter dated March 4th from Mr Jelavic, and I have provided the Prosecutor with a copy of that letter, and in that letter he purports to tell me what he has done in compliance with my order. I would like to hear from the Prosecutor first regarding its position with respect to this order directing Mr Jelavic to provide these documents and to advise the Prosecutor of the location of the documents, if he did not produce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I can report to the Court that we have not received a single document in response to your order of 24th -- I am sorry, of 28th February, and, in response to the subpoena duces tecum. Additionally, your Honour, we have not been provided immediate access to the documents contained in the Central Archive of what was formerly the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So, in our view, your Honour, this letter which has been received and which I have reviewed does not constitute compliance with a Court Order. I would submit also, your Honour, that the failure of Mr Jelavic to provide the Court with the exact location or locations of these documents also is a failure on his part, and our view is that there has been non-compliance with your Order, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs Glumac? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Your Honour, I would just like to present you one document which is dated 21st February 1997, and I ask that it be placed on the record. It is a letter of the Prime Minister Edhem Bicakcic in which he asked the Office for Legislative Affairs to take over the archive of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosnia. So, from that letter, you can see that he has recognised what we have stated before, that Mr Jelavic is not legal successor of the archive of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a Minister of Defence, and he is tasking another person to take over the said archive. This letter is addressed to the secretary, Mrs Valerija Galic, and the Office of the Legislative Affairs of the Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I would kindly request that this letter be placed on the record. It is clear from the letter that the Ministry of Defence is not only -- not only that it is not the legal successor of the archive, but it also says that Mr Jelavic and the Ministry of Defence are not competent to take over the archive of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosnia. This is the letter dated 21st February 1997, but notwithstanding this letter, Mr Jelavic, because the Minister of the Federation does not possess the archive, he issued two orders, requesting that all commanders of military districts and commanders of brigades and administration of the headquarters of the HVO must collect and classify all available archival material from the homeland war and that the priority should be given to the period from 1st April 1992 until 1st January 1994. This material should be promptly dispatched to the premises of the Croatian defence counsel in Mostar not later than 15th March 1997. There is another order, which was issued on 4th March 1997. He requested that all the request archival material that is collected on the basis of the first order should be safeguarded and protected, and Mr Ante Jelavic has tasked military commanders of military districts to be responsible to carry out to implement that order. Therefore, on 15th March 1997, this documentation will be made available to the Tribunal. It will be made available to the person authorised by you to revise that documentation, copy all the necessary material and take it over. The only thing that remains maybe disputable is what we requested last time that the Tribunal address a letter to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the Civilian Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces, and the request that this material be handed over to the Tribunal. We are talking about classified material, very confidential material, military secrets mostly, and most of that material has an impact to the security of the state. Therefore, we would kindly ask the Tribunal to send a letter to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, in that way, to enable Mr Jelavic to hand over the documentation to the Tribunal. All the relevant documents can be found in the military districts and military commanders of districts are responsible for that documentation. Therefore, that documentation can be found there, but the Presidency must authorise that documentation to be handed over to the Tribunal. I do not think that there will be any problems about that. I would just like to mention that the handing over of such documents in Bosnia and Herzegovina represents a criminal offence of disclosing a military secret, unless there is an authorisation of the relevant authority. So, in order to prevent any kind of abuse and in order to avoid Mr Jelavic having legal problems, I would kindly ask the Tribunal to send such a letter. The deadline was too short, I am afraid, the deadline of 28th February, so we would kindly ask to extend it until 15th March, which is the only realistic possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mrs Glumac, I have a couple of questions. I really do not understand what you have said with respect to that date of March 15th. Are you saying that, by that date, Mr Jelavic will provide the Prosecutor with the documents that are the subject of the subpoena duces tecum, if I issue a letter to the Presidency of the Federation? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does Mr Jelavic consider that he needs direction from the Federation in order to turn over the documents? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): This is the instruction from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the Civilian Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces of the Federation, pursuant to Article 5 of the Institution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Article 22 of the law on the defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, the civilian, the Supreme Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces in Bosnia is the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And can you give me the name of the person to whom this request is to be made? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): The President is Mr Alija Izetbegovic and members of the Presidency are Mr Kresimir Zubak and Mr Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that Mr Izetbegovic would make the decision as to whether or not these documents are to be turned over? Is it his responsibility. MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Yes, the Presidency should be in charge of reaching such a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is that Mr Izetbegovic? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): All three of them, all three persons that I have mentioned that have -- they must pass decisions unanimously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have discussed this at the last hearing in terms of who was responsible. Of course Mr Jelavic has received a letter, at least two letters from the Prime Minister, directing him to turn over these documents. I gather it is still your position that the Prime Minister is without authority. It is the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency, that has that authority? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Well, he is in a very particular situation, because he is a Civilian Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces, not in his capacity of a minister. There is another institution above him, which is at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the level of the Federation. It is him. But at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is the Presidency. As I say, this is pursuant to the constitution and the law on the defence. Aside from that, I would also like to mention that Prime Minister Bicakcic has asked Mr Jelavic to hand over the documents, but we also have a letter in which he requested a different institution to take over the archive of the Croatian Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I am talking about the Office for Legislative Affairs of the Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the letter that I would like to be placed on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That will be made Jelavic Exhibit 1. Do you have a translation of that letter into English? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Unfortunately, we did not have enough time to translate it. We received it only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Who is the head of the Office of Legislative Affairs? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): The head of the office, the general secretary of the office is Mrs Valerija Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Even though the Prime Minister then has, you have indicated, transferred responsibility for these documents to the Office of Legislative Affairs, Mr Jelavic, you are telling me, is willing to turn over these documents by March 15th; is that correct? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Yes, provided that he receives an authorisation from the Presidency. He really wishes to co-operate with the Tribunal, and this is something that we have mentioned already, that we mentioned last time. If he had been summoned to appear in some other capacity, and pursuant to a different order, maybe the order which is -- maybe as an Amicus Curiae, I am sure that he would have appeared before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What is his relationship with the Office of Legislative Affairs? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Well, he actually does not have anything, any special relations with that office, because the Office for Legislative Affairs functions as part of the Ministry of Justice, and he is Minister of Defence. Therefore, this is a completely different institution. This is a different ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I suppose I do not understand again what you have told me. On the one hand, you tell me that he does not have control or responsibility for these documents, that the Prime Minister on 21st has transferred responsibility for these documents to the Office of Legislative Affairs, and then you tell me, however, he will turn them over by March 15th, if a letter is directed to the Federation, or an order, or a request, from me, and the Federation then directs that he turn these documents over. I suppose that those are internal problems or procedures within the Federation that I really have no control over, and no knowledge of. They also seem to be inconsistent to me. As far as Mr Jelavic's failure to appear here, because I issued a subpoena duces tecum as opposed to a request for him to appear as Amicus Curiae, once again I do not understand that. The question is his responsibility to be here regardless of how this request is styled, whether it is in the form of a subpoena or whether it is in the form of a request for him to appear as Amicus Curiae. The point is that several requests have been made to Mr Jelavic to appear, and he has failed to do that. MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Well, I can answer to the first part of your -- what I said is the fact that he is not responsible for the archives, and then later on we claim that we are prepared to make available those documents. I would just like to say that there are no inconsistencies here. He is not the custodian of the archive. The Ministry of Defence possesses only the archive that was established on 22nd December 1996, when Mr Jelavic took over the Ministry of Defence of the Federation. So, before that -- and the Ministry of Defence of the Federation has not yet taken over the archive, and he never had any function in relation to that archive. He cannot hand over that archive, because he does not have it. He is willing to hand over the documentation, which is in the possession of the HVO troops, who were in charge of issuing such orders. Therefore, the documentation, which is in the possession of military commanders of the commanders of military districts, that documentation is identical to the documentation which can be found in the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But you are saying, then, that he is responsible for the documents that are in the possession of the HVO units? He does have control over those documents? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): He was not Minister of Defence at the time of war, and he only recently became Minister of Defence of the Federation. He does not exactly know what is where. He simply requested that all the ministry documentation that is in the possession of the HVO troops and its military commanders be dispatched to Mostar to the premises of the HVO and he also ordered that that documentation be inspected, classified and forwarded to the Tribunal. Therefore, during the war until 1994, he was never in charge of the archives, and he was appointed Minister of Defence at the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: These orders that he has entered, I think there are two that are made reference to, do you have copies of those orders? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Will you provide me with copies of those orders as well? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So then Mr Jelavic does have the sufficient control over the HVO units to obtain the military documentation that they have, and that is what these two orders do, is direct that they transfer that to Mostar and classify it. That is the documentation that he will provide by March 15th. MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Mrs Vidovic? MRS VIDOVIC (in interpretation): I would like to explain again the issues that were raised in the last status conference hearing. Pursuant to the law on federal institutions, the documentation belonging to the HVO should have been transferred to control of the archive of the Federation and from everything that we have heard here, it is clear that this transfer, on the part of the HVO, has not been affected, and that these documents are still in the possession of the HVO. From the letter of Mr Jelavic quoted today, it is clear that he issued an order to the units of the HVO to collect these archival materials and transfer it to the HVO command in Mostar. From this order, it is clear that Mr Jelavic has authority over these units and over the material. From the letter of the Prime Minister Bicakcic, it is clear that he is attempting to comply with the orders of the Tribunal and he is requesting of Mr Jelavic to transfer these documents and make them available to the Tribunal, so that does not mean that Mr Bicakcic is not holding Mr Jelavic responsible for these documents. I would like to clarify one thing. The state of Bosnia and Herzegovina has recognised the authority of the Tribunal in The Hague and its primacy in the matters relating to the crimes as described through the Statute of the Tribunal and its rules. In no law of Bosnia and Herzegovina is there any provision that prevents any Government body or official from turning over any documents to the Tribunal. It includes the documents that constitute official state secrets, and the only proviso and the only request that the law puts forth is that the Tribunal complies with its own statute and keep those secrets. In other words, these documents that are the subject of the subpoena duces tecum should be turned over, because Bosnia and Herzegovina have recognised the authority of the tribunal and it has also agreed to make these documents available to the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: My concern is something that has been discussed previously at at least two hearings, and that is the responsibility for these documents, really the body who is the superior to the Minister of Defence. You have indicated, Mrs Vidovic, previously that the Prime Minister has the authority to direct the Minister of Defence to act. Mrs Glumac has said once again, as she said at the last hearing that, no, it is the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The subpoena is addressed to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I perhaps will hear from the Prosecutor with respect to this responsibility, but it seems to me that it is inappropriate for me to become involved with this question of who has the responsibility. We look to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the subpoena is directed to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Prime Minister has directed Mr Jelavic to provide the documents, and I am really somewhat reluctant now to go to another authority to request those very documents when I have, in the record, at least two letters from the Prime Minister telling Mr Jelavic to comply. Mrs Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MRS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: I did not have the translation, but I understand. Something happened here. It is on 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What I am saying is that, once again, the subpoenas have been directed to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Prime Minister has indicated that Mr Jelavic should comply, and now you are suggesting that we proceed again, I gather the Prosecutor would have to issue a new subpoena addressed to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what you are saying needs to be done? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): No, I do not think that that needs to be done. I think that the Prime Minister Bicakcic confirms our theory that there has been no direct legal succession leading to the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the legal basis which is also recognised by Mr Bicakcic. In other words, he is now looking for a different person through this Office for Legislative Affairs of the Government who can take over this responsibility, since the archives of the Herceg-Bosna was not only a military archive but a wider archive and did not deal exclusively with military documents and affairs. So, in other words, another person needs to be designated and another Government agency identified, which will take over and take control of these archives. There is an Office for Legislative Affairs who can help determine who this person or who this agency should be. As I said, this involves not only military archival material, but the civilian as well. What we are seeking here is not -- we would like to see that Mr Bicakcic takes a decision. We see that he has a dilemma too, and we are seeing that the documents are being collected, the military documents are being collected, and we need an authorisation of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as is provided by the constitution and by the law, because they are the Civilian Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces, and the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is also subject to their decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The letter -- and I do not have it before me at this point -- as I recall, from our last hearing, there was a letter from the Prime Minister to Mr Jelavic that transferred responsibility for the military documents that were a part of the archives to Mr Jelavic, and, as I recall it at the last hearing we had, you indicated that this letter then stands for the proposition that he never had authority before, but, as of the date of that letter, he was given responsibility for the military documents that were a part of the archives. If you stand by -- if I am correct in that statement, and I think I am, and in what you said -- if that is true, then he does now have authority for the military documents that were a part of the archives. The letter dated February 21st must have been before the letters that we had and discussed at our last hearing from the Prime Minister to Mr Jelavic. So, without getting too much involved in the internal affairs, it seems to me that perhaps what has happened is that the non-military records have been transferred, or at least have been placed under the control of the Office of Legislative Affairs, but that the military documents that were a part of the archive of Herceg-Bosna are now under the control of Mr Jelavic. Am I correct? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): That is a good interpretation, but that is not how things are usually handled where we are. These archives were not formally divided so that somebody would come and say, "This is the civilian side and somebody will take charge of that and somebody will take control of the military side". Nobody has turned over the control of these archives either to the Ministry of Defence or to any other Government agency. The only thing that we have here is this letter directing the office to take control of these archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But at the last hearing, as I recall, you had accepted the authority of the Prime Minister to direct that Mr Jelavic assume responsibility for the defence documents, and at the last hearing you indicated, well, this is the first time that he has been given this authority, and I think the letter may have been dated, I do not know, February 28th. Let us see if we can find it. No, it is dated February 24th. Only from this date does he have that authority. So, if you accept that the Prime Minister has sufficient authority to make Mr Jelavic responsible for the defence documents that were formerly in the archive of Herceg-Bosna, it seems to me that that issue has been foreclosed, and I do not know why we have to begin to discuss the Federation. MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): The matter has now been resolved, because in the last hearing we requested for the transfer of the documents by Mr Jelavic. We also request a decision by the Presidency, and that was a request that was directed to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As far as the documents containing any state secrets, as was indicated by Miss Vidovic, I, of course, would receive the documents, and I would place them under seal, and I would review them in camera, without the presence of the Prosecutor, to determine whether, in fact, they do contain any state secrets that should not be disclosed to the Prosecutor. Does that satisfy your concern about the documents containing state secrets? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): Mr Jelavic, as Minister of Defence, is of opinion that, given the legislation within the state and the provisions of the constitution and the law on the Armed Forces, that he has no problem with turning over these documents but he needs an authorisation, because there is a provision in the law about the criminal offence of disclosing state secrets, and it is only the Presidency that can rule on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to raise a number of points, your Honour. The first is there is an HVO archive, and that has been acknowledged in previous submissions, because Mr Jelavic has informed this court that the previous archivist, Mr Brkcic, died an untimely and unnatural death in, I believe, November. So that archive, in fact, exists. It is somewhere, and we have not had a single answer from Mr Jelavic as to where that archive is, despite our repeated efforts to locate or have him inform us where those archives are. In respect of the letter that has been referred to by counsel, I have a translation of that letter which I would ask to be passed up to you, your Honour. What this letter in its translated form says, it is a letter from Mr Bicakcic to Mrs Galic, who is from the Office of Legislative Affairs, and it says, according to this translation, and I quote: "Since the archive of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has not yet been set up, and in the interest of prompt compliance with the ICTY order, it is necessary that you take immediate and appropriate measures for the transfer of documents from the archive of the HVO HZ-HB." This again is another acknowledgement that this archive exists. The archive did not fall into a vacuum with the death of the previous custodian, and Mr Jelavic, who has acknowledged that he has control over HVO documents, we have been informed, on previous occasions, he also has control over this archive. The suggestion that has been made by Mr Jelavic in his letter, dated 4th March, that he will ask for military HVO officers to go through their materials and find documents and send them to Mostar clearly will not respond completely to the subpoena, because the subpoena, which was issued on January 15th, has a total of 19 items. Clearly his officers in the field will not have access to these documents. These documents, we believe, are either located in the central archives, or -- and I would be very interested in a clarification on this point -- are there also a separate HVO military archives? I would request the Court ask counsel if such a separate archives exist, because what we are interested in, in this subpoena, is access to all of the documents that are contained in the subpoena duces tecum. Your Honour, in respect of the request by Mr Jelavic to your Honour to write a letter to his Presidency, it seems to me that is inappropriate. It seems to me your Honour has directed a Court Order to Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is incumbent on the Government to sort out the problem that is described by Mr Jelavic in his letter to you. I do not see where it is necessary to get involved in that. The order is a sufficient request to this Court. I also believe, your Honour, that these documents, it is incumbent that these documents be turned over to the Court, that the Office of the Prosecutor not be dispatched to a location in Bosnia and Herzegovina to collect them. My own view is they should be sent to this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The documents that Mr Jelavic is willing to provide by March 15th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If I may, your Honour, I have a copy of a translation of this letter, which I would like the usher to pass up to you, and I also have additional exhibits for today's hearing, which I will describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The three documents that Mrs Glumac has provided will be marked Jelavic Exhibits 1, 2 and 3. You had the two orders that you have provided, Mrs Glumac, as well as the letter of February 21st, and those will be marked and admitted. What do you wish to offer, Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would wish to offer a letter which is addressed to me from Judge Vidovic, and it informs me of what happened in respect of your last order, what she did with the order, and when it was served on Mr Jelavic. There are, attached to her letter describing that, a total of four sheets of paper showing proofs of service on respective ministers. So if I may introduce this as a single exhibit and pass these up to you as well, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit 1, and we have made the letter from Mr Jelavic to me dated March 1st a Court Exhibit, have we not? If not, we should. We have. Mr Harmon, do you have additional exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional exhibits, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I firmly believe we are again finding ourselves with no exhibits and not in compliance with the order of this Court in the previous efforts to obtain information about locations of these archives, obtain documents, and I believe that Mr Jelavic has not complied with this Court Order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And how do you wish us to proceed at this point? I entered on February 28th an order to ensure compliance with the subpoena duces tecum, and I indicated in that order that, if Mr Jelavic did not comply with the two requests, that is, to advise me of the exact location of the documents by March 4th, and also to provide the documents to me by March 5th, or alternatively provide the Prosecutor with access, that if he failed to do that, then he was to appear today at 10.00 am to show cause why he should not be held in contempt for failure to comply. Mr Jelavic is not here, and I will find that he has not complied with that order. The letter of March 4th does not comply with the February 28th order. So how do we proceed at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request, then, that we have a hearing in order to show cause why he should not be held in contempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Before setting that hearing, if that is how we are to proceed, a number of questions have been raised as a result of the subpoenas that were issued which I had signed in January addressed to Croatia and to the Defence Minister of Croatia, Mr Susak, and the second subpoena was addressed to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to the Minister of Defence, Mr Ante Jelavic. The representative from Croatia is not here today, because we were not to consider that issue. Croatia, when they appeared, the Ambassador, Mr Salaj, appeared. He agreed that he would notify the Prosecutor by Monday, February 24th, as I recall, of a date to arrange a meeting with the appropriate representatives to locate the documents that were the subject of that subpoena. That meeting was to take place on February 28th, as I recall. That has not been resolved as well. I presume the meeting took place, although there has been no report, no formal report made to me, and there is no representative present today from Croatia, but both of these subpoenas raise issues that I would like to have briefed by the parties, first of all, by the Prosecution, and I would invite Croatia, and I will do that in an order, since the representative is not present, to also brief the issues that I think are raised by both subpoenas. The first issue relates to the power of a judge of the tribunal to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a state. The second issue relates to the power of a judge of a Trial Chamber to issue a subpoena duces tecum to an official of the state, and the third issue relates to what remedies are appropriate if there is non-compliance with these subpoenas. The reason that I am asking for this briefing is that the subpoena that was addressed to Croatia and the Defence Minister has really not been resolved. The subpoena that has been addressed to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mr Jelavic, we have been moving along on that, but really very unsuccessfully, Mrs Glumac, I would have to say, because I really get the impression that there are relationships within Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that I really cannot become involved in. The subpoena is addressed to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have, on the record, at least two letters from the Prime Minister directing Mr Jelavic to respond, and he says no, he will not respond, because the Prime Minister does not have authority. That is something that I really cannot resolve. All I can do is to sign the subpoena that was addressed to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to Mr Jelavic, and, if Mr Jelavic feels that he cannot comply, that does not excuse him from coming to the Tribunal to explain that, and whether that request is made of him in the form of a subpoena, or a request to appear as Amicus Curiae, I am not really concerned. I want him here, and, if I truly believed that he would be here if I requested that he appear as an Amicus Curiae, I would not really, in principle, have a problem with that, because we really want to get to the bottom line, however we get to the bottom line, but, in all honesty, I do not believe that he would appear if I asked him to appear as an Amicus Curiae. Most importantly, regardless of this conflict, as you pose, between the authority of the Prime Minister and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency of the Federation, Mrs Vidovic takes a different position, and she says that the Prime Minister has the authority and she is the liaison with the Tribunal on matters like this, and all I can do is accept her representations because I know nothing of the internal relations between the Federation and the Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So all I can do is accept her representations that he has the authority, and he has told him to be here and he is not. We can, I suppose, set a date for the hearing for Mr Jelavic to show cause why he should not be held in contempt, and we can also set a date for the submission of briefs on these issues and the argument, if argument is to be presented, on the issues that I have suggested. What would you suggest, Mr Harmon, in terms of the settings? I would suggest that we have the briefing and arguments on the issues before I set a hearing, or I can do it the other way round. I could set a hearing to determine whether Mr Jelavic should be held in contempt before we receive the briefing and before we have oral arguments, or I can set it after. You tell me how you wish me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would set it after the argument and the briefs. That would provide Mr Jelavic still another occasion to comply with the subpoena as directed to him to provide all the documents contained in the subpoena duces tecum, and it may mute the issue of contempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I very well may enter another order, then, regarding Mr Jelavic's response through his legal counsel, or I may not. I may just suspend this matter and consider setting a hearing on the order to show cause why he should not be held in contempt after the arguments. How long do you need to brief this issue, Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am certain we could provide you with briefs the week before argument. I would respectfully request that argument in this matter take place on 16th April, and I do not have a calendar in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is a Wednesday, and you have two weeks before then. Today is March 7th. Why do I not set March 28th, or we could say the Monday, March 31st, for the filing of briefs? That would be briefs by the Prosecution on these issues, briefs by Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whoever wishes to submit briefs on that date as well, and I will ask that Croatia, if it so desires and wishes to advance the position that it took at an earlier hearing, regarding the absence of authority to issue a subpoena to a state or to a high governmental official, that they submit briefs as well by March 31st, but I will do that in a separate order. Mr Bos tells me that March 31st is Easter Monday and that is a holiday, so I suppose no one will be here at the tribunal, except me. I will be here. So, then, we will make it April 1st the briefs will be filed, by all parties, and then, if a reply brief by any of the parties wishes to be filed, the reply then should be filed by April 7th, and we will tentatively set arguments on these issues for April 16th at 10.00 am. Unfortunately we only have one courtroom. Maybe that will change one day soon, but on that date, in April, there will be at least one trial proceeding. So I will tentatively set the date for March 16th, and we will confirm it with the parties as soon as I have an opportunity to confer with the other Trial Chamber. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be perfectly clear, the subpoena then remains in effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The subpoena remains in effect. The findings that I made in the order of February 24th, I believe -- no, let me see, February 28th, remain in effect. What I am not doing at this time is setting a date for the hearing on the order to show cause. Or we could set a date in April for that if you wish, Mr Harmon. Perhaps we should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On reflection, your Honour, I think it might be a very good idea to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will postpone, then, that particular issue, and consider it on April 18th at 10.00 as well, and what that means is that I will enter another order directing that Mr Jelavic appear, either in his capacity as Minister of Defence, or in his official capacity as Minister of Defence, or, if he wishes to consider himself an Amicus Curiae, whatever he wants to call himself, he should be here on April 18th at 10.00 am, to show cause why he should not be held in contempt, because he has been directed, at least on three different occasions. So I hope that you make that very clear to him, Mrs Glumac. Once again, the trial will be proceeding, and so those dates have been set, April 16th at 10.00 am and April 18th at 10.00 am, but, if there is a change because of the use of our one courtroom, then I will notify the parties. Is there anything else, Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Anything else, Mrs Glumac? Do you have anything further to add? MRS GLUMAC (in interpretation): No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mrs Vidovic. MRS VIDOVIC (in interpretation): No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then we will stand adjourned. (11.05 am) (Tribunal Adjourned) 24 25
